## Groundtrack

Use Groundtrack as the shared engineering memory for this repository.

- At session start, check whether Groundtrack tools are available, using tool discovery if the client supports it. If `search_experiences` is unavailable, or a Groundtrack call reports connection, sign-in, or hook-setup problems, tell the user promptly, once per session unless the problem changes. Give the setup command for the current agent from this repository's root, for example `npx --yes --package @groundtrack/hooks@latest groundtrack setup --agent codex` when running in Codex. If the current agent is unclear, omit `--agent` to use the picker. Continue the user's task; when Groundtrack cannot be used, say so rather than claiming a successful lookup or inventing retrieved experiences.
- Before non-trivial investigation or implementation where prior decisions, failures, or constraints could matter, call `search_experiences`. Start with a focused description of the work, then inspect the results and search one or two materially different adjacent concepts when related components, constraints, failure modes, or prior decisions could change the approach. Do not stop merely because the first search has no exact match; try a meaningfully broader or neighboring query. Keep this expansion bounded, and also search before repeating an approach that may already have been tried.
- When a relevant experience needs more context or verification, call `get_experience_events` with its id to inspect the underlying raw evidence and provenance.
- Apply relevant current experiences and heed any caveats that an experience was contradicted, superseded, or expired.
- Only call `report_experience_use` if `search_experiences` returned experiences; skip it for empty results, even with a retrieval id. For non-empty results, report when one changed the approach or avoided a failure, and report `not_helpful` after review when none applied.
- After a task reaches a concrete result, call `record_outcome` with a short title, a concise summary, and the retrieval ids for searches that contributed. Include measurements only for sourced, quantified impact on time, cost, reliability, quality, performance, or throughput; tests, typechecks, lint, and builds are validation rather than impact. Include avoided work only when it was explicitly estimated, and never infer unknown values.
- After a non-obvious discovery, decision, workaround, correction, or failed approach that would help a future agent, call `store_event` promptly with a concise title and an explanation of what happened and why it matters.
- Do not store routine implementation details, obvious facts, unrestricted transcripts, or secrets.
- Keep the raw-event ids returned by `store_event`. When the related work lands in a commit or pull request, call `link_outcomes` with those ids and the explicit commit SHA and/or pull-request number. Never infer an outcome from worktree HEAD.

<!-- groundtrack:end -->

name: groundtrack-impact
description: Audit local Claude Code and Codex histories for evidence-backed knowledge-use stories and initiative-driven environment changes. Use only when the user explicitly invokes this skill and authorizes local session access.
---

# Groundtrack impact

Answer “How has Groundtrack concretely helped me?” with an at-a-glance value summary followed by specific stories. This is a user-invoked, read-only local audit, not the server-side Impact Analyst or a causal ROI study. Make the strongest supportable positive case, including all defensible instances rather than stopping after finding a few examples.

## Scope and privacy

- Confirm explicit authorization to read local coding sessions. Use requested agents, repositories, and dates; otherwise cover **all locally available** Claude Code and Codex sessions on this machine, including archived sessions and subagents. State the actual scope and unavailable history. For a large corpus, spend the time to audit it; do not silently substitute a recent sample. If authorization is absent, ask before opening transcripts.
- Read session files in place. Do not import or upload transcripts, use write-capable Groundtrack tools (including feedback or outcome recording), mutate repositories, or save transcript copies. Never run Groundtrack's session-import command. A hosted agent may send selected content to its model provider during analysis; do not claim device-only processing.
- Keep private prompts, credentials, raw local paths, and unrelated transcript content out of the customer-facing report. Paraphrase sensitive details. Supporting record/PR links are useful where available, but exact citations are a recommendation, not a gate.

## Census and audit

1. Freeze an ISO UTC cutoff at the start of the audit and pass the same `--until TIMESTAMP` to all scanner/evidence runs; exclude the audit's own later activity from the report. Run `node scripts/scan.mjs --until TIMESTAMP` from this skill directory (or pass `--since YYYY-MM-DD` to both scripts for an explicitly requested UTC event-time window; `--codex-home` and `--claude-home` can point at alternate local homes). The scanner only reads local JSONL and emits an inventory of structured Groundtrack-call candidates, file locations, line numbers, and coverage. It does not identify impact. Record found, readable, unparseable, and missing histories, plus candidate and noncandidate sessions by agent. Its wrapper-call matches are **leads**: inspect the actual call and result to reject quoted code, unsuccessful calls, duplicates, or setup-only activity. If the scanner cannot run, perform an equivalent full inventory using the supported session locations and disclose what was not covered.
2. Run `node scripts/evidence.mjs --until TIMESTAMP` for a compact per-session index of feedback and outcomes; `--reports` lists feedback leads, `--session ID` shows a session's evidence rows, and `--chains` joins the latest successful helpful verdict per retrieval to successful outcomes by retrieval ID and to asserted PR/commit links by raw-event ID. The index exposes both raw `helpedReports` and `currentHelpfulRetrievals` after corrections; use the latter for a current positive-feedback session count. The parser never executes transcript code and never determines impact. **Do not report its raw counts as ROI.** Check the actual call result, the retrieval it refers to, and neighboring work before accepting a feedback claim. Verify PR merge/deployment status, whether a link was accepted or pending, and later reversals with read-only checks. A PR mentioned nearby in a long chat is not a join. Distinguish historically merged work from still-surviving work, especially after a feature was reverted or removed.
3. Triage **every Groundtrack-active session in scope**, not merely the most recent or most promising: review its actual structured calls/results, feedback verdicts, outcomes, and Review leads, including setup-only sessions and later corrections. Then inspect neighboring transcript context around **every plausible distinct positive work-item lead**, from initial retrieval or finding through action and outcome; do not treat index rows alone as impact. `node scripts/context.mjs FILE LINE [RADIUS]` displays a bounded excerpt at an evidence-row location; it may contain sensitive text and is for local analysis only. Include retrievals, feedback, outcomes, initiatives, and Review activity even if the latter has no `search_experiences` call. Flag impact-audit/evaluation sessions already in the historical corpus: include them in coverage but exclude their self-referential feedback and outcomes from the customer-value numerator. Join repeated calls on the same issue; a single long session or repeated feedback must not inflate a count. Build a private evidence ledger with a stable issue/work-item key, source session(s), actual Groundtrack evidence, the earlier plan or code, subsequent action, validation, outcome, and claim level. Do not put raw transcript text in this ledger or the report. Report both `sessions triaged / Groundtrack-active sessions` and `positive work items deeply checked`; if plausible leads remain unchecked, label the benefit count a verified lower bound, not an exhaustive total.
4. Consult available **read-only** Groundtrack evidence for candidate retrievals, experiences and raw events, feedback, outcomes, initiatives, and Review findings. Check corrections, contradictions, supersessions, and whether a warning originated earlier in the same session. Local session context is primary evidence of changed behavior; backend feedback alone is not. Groundtrack's backend index may be incomplete, so never use it as the denominator for all coding sessions. If a detail source is unavailable, count only what local evidence supports and note the gap briefly.
5. Classify each distinct issue/work item once at its highest supported level:
   - **Verified defect detected or fixed**: Groundtrack's specific retrieval, prior experience, or Review finding directed an investigation that revealed a real defect, or identified it directly. The session shows the subsequent fix and independent confirmation (test, merged fix, deployment check, or actual failure matching the prediction). Distinguish pre-merge catches from production incidents diagnosed after deployment; never imply that an incident was prevented if it happened.
   - **Mistake caught before completion**: a concrete risky plan or implementation is visible _before_ Groundtrack surfaced the relevant warning/finding; the subsequent session shows a targeted correction; and code, tests, review, or another independent artifact corroborates the change. Count observed interceptions, not hypothetical production incidents or failures that “would have shipped.” A generic warning or a preexisting fix does not qualify. A verified defect that was caught here belongs to the previous bucket, not both.
   - **Other observed course correction**: a specific Groundtrack retrieval or Review finding preceded and informed a visible decision or change, but the earlier approach was not demonstrably a mistake or independent verification is missing.
   - **Agent-reported help only**: explicit helpful-use feedback without a traceable changed action. Report separately, never as a prevented mistake.
   - **Retrieved / reviewed only**: no demonstrated help; keep in the denominator, not a positive numerator. Do not turn “work completed after retrieval” into causal credit.
     One issue belongs to only one bucket. Separate **verified completion** (merged fix, deployed work, passing validation, or an outcome tied to the issue) from the help bucket; completion is a parallel attribute, not another additive impact count. Count Review-only work with the same rules. Check that superficially similar cases are distinct before aggregating. An `avoided_failure` feedback effect is a lead, never sufficient evidence of prevention: check whether the agent had already found or fixed the same issue before retrieval.
6. For before/after, look at comparable local pre-Groundtrack tasks if the history actually contains them. Report the comparable population and a descriptive contrast; changes in task mix, agent, or observability invalidate a causal efficiency claim. Time, money, tokens, and avoided incidents require separately sourced measurements or explicit estimates. Never invent a subscription ROI multiple.

## Initiative impact (separate, optional)

After the knowledge-loop audit, search read-only Groundtrack initiatives using the recurring friction and system changes found in the local sessions. Inspect current initiative detail (`search_initiatives` then `get_initiative` when available), including supporting and opposing events, relationships, dates, and linked outcomes; follow the local coding sessions and actual PR/deployment evidence. Verify that the initiative preceded or shaped the claimed intervention; a record created after a completed fix is retrospective context, not proof Groundtrack drove it. Search results, initiative state, an agent's attribution, or a `resolved` label alone do not establish implementation or impact. Check whether an apparent fix is a partial slice, was later replaced, or had a subsequent recurrence. The backend index may omit detail; use it as a lead, not a complete initiative census.

Classify only credible, distinct initiative stories:

- **Realized environment improvement:** recurring friction is documented; Groundtrack surfaced or organized a specific initiative; the intended system change landed; and comparable, time-ordered evidence after deployment shows that the same failure mode declined or stopped over a stated observation window. Describe the exposure and observation limits. Silence, a green test, or an absence of later search hits is not a measured decline, and the initiative must not receive sole causal credit when other interventions contributed.
- **Implemented but unverified:** a clearly linked intervention landed and its immediate behavior may be validated, but later recurrence has not been measured sufficiently. State the implemented scope and what would verify durable improvement. A proposed initiative can fall here when independent code/PR evidence proves implementation; its state alone cannot.
- **Identified opportunity:** a draft or proposal identifies a recurring, supported problem and a prospective intervention, but that intervention has not landed. Partial progress that leaves the stated failure mode open must be described as partial, not realized. Never count a draft or proposal as an achieved improvement.

Keep initiative trajectory separate from retrieval/Review work-item attribution. If the same PR, defect, or change appears in both tracks, tell one story with an initiative label or cross-reference it; count the work item once in the headline, and never add initiative totals to defect or safeguard totals. Include a compact initiative section only when at least one story survives this audit; omit it entirely when none does, rather than padding the report with initiative counts. An identified opportunity is a next step, not realized value.

## Report

Start with a short, positive **at-a-glance** line or compact scorecard containing the strongest supportable numbers. When available, put broad **reach** (historically merged/deployed changes with a traceable Groundtrack chain, sessions with current positive agent feedback) beside **demonstrated changed work** (distinct completed work items, verified fixes split pre-merge/post-deploy, concrete mistakes caught before completion, and other course corrections). The largest defensible reach number can lead, but label it as reach in the same glance that identifies the smaller, stronger changed-work count; never imply the counts are additive or equally causal. Do not open with file/session inventory, triage methodology, or a wall of caveats. Use real numbers, including zero when fully audited; use “at least” and a partial denominator if coverage is incomplete.

For reach, count only historically merged/deployed changes with an explicit retrieval → latest successful helpful feedback verdict → outcome → raw-event → PR/commit chain, after checking tool-call success and the claimed PR/revision. This **usage footprint** is not a count of prevented failures, current functionality, or ROI. Keep agent-reported-only help distinct from demonstrated changes, exclude self-audits from value numerators, deduplicate issues across sessions, and disclose historical work later removed.

Then tell a few memorable, strongest stories up front and group other checked examples by recurring failure mode, with enough compact detail to substantiate the headline. Each should explain the task, the Groundtrack evidence, the agent's visible change, and what followed; identify whether the issue was caught before merge, repaired after deployment, or was a design/release safeguard. Favor cross-session reuse and non-Groundtrack work among equally strong cases. Offer useful evidence links when available. Put the nuanced distinction (reported / observed / verified) in compact labels and make the value clear without repetitive hedging. If a claim does not survive audit, omit it from positive stories rather than padding the report with weak anecdotes. If an initiative story qualifies, label its category and put it after or alongside the relevant work-item story without increasing the headline work-item count; state the implementation and recurrence evidence separately.

When the same failure mode recurs in **distinct work items**, add a concise pattern line such as “Cross-user access mistakes caught in 3 separate changes,” with the three issue keys and corroborating records available on request. A repeated warning or feedback in one work item counts once, and a taxonomy match alone is not proof that each intervention changed the work.

End with a brief scope note: `N/M Groundtrack-active sessions triaged; K distinct work items deeply checked; A/B total local sessions screened` (by agent if useful), local histories missing or unaudited, unavailable backend detail, and any comparable baseline. Name the most actionable instrumentation gap. If no positive case survives, do not fabricate one: report the completed census, what evidence is missing, and a concrete path to a stronger future measurement.

# @groundtrack/hooks

Set up Groundtrack across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode in one flow.
Node.js 18 or newer is required.

```sh
npx --yes --package @groundtrack/hooks@latest groundtrack setup
```

Choose the agents you use, review the changes, and finish any sign-in or hook
approval shown for each agent. The picker detects both machine installations
and project configuration. Your choices are remembered; adding Codex later
preserves your working Claude and Cursor connections.

```sh
groundtrack setup --agent codex
groundtrack setup --agent claude --agent codex --agent cursor --yes
groundtrack setup --all-detected --yes
groundtrack setup --agent codex --dry-run
groundtrack status
groundtrack status --json
```

`--agent` is repeatable. `--client` and `claude-code` are accepted aliases.
Setup configures the current project; it does not activate Groundtrack in every
repository. Use `--repo PATH` to choose a project and `--url URL` for another
Groundtrack endpoint. With no explicit targets, an interactive terminal shows
the picker. An unattended `--yes` run needs a previously saved selection or
explicit `--agent` / `--all-detected`; it never falls back to all known agents.
An empty selection or cancellation makes no changes.

Setup also enrolls the explicitly configured Git project in the native repository
registry and installs per-user background **preview** workers for selected Codex,
Claude Code and Cursor agents. The same service manager works with all three adapters.
Workers start at login, survive terminal closure and restart after crashes. macOS
uses LaunchAgents, Linux uses systemd user units, and Windows uses per-user logon
tasks; no administrator/root installation is required. Linux requires a working
systemd user session and glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, for both x64
and arm64 packaged binaries). Windows ARM and other unlisted native targets are not supported.

Windows task names include the current user's SID so accounts on the same machine
cannot take over one another's workers. `service install --no-start` installs jobs
disabled at login; use `service start` to enable them later.

The setup preview/confirmation includes this machine-level change. `--yes`
includes background setup for the explicitly selected agents. Use `--no-service`
to configure only MCP/hooks. An explicitly stopped worker remains stopped on
subsequent setup runs. Official npm releases bundle the version-pinned native
binaries, check their SHA-256 and version, and copy the matching executable to a stable, private,
content-addressed location outside the npm cache. A failed service installation
is reported separately from saved agent configuration and makes setup exit nonzero.
No transcript uploads, API keys, background OAuth, or durable import state are
introduced by service installation.
`doctor --fix` continues to repair only MCP/hooks; it does not implicitly add
background collection. Use setup or the explicit service install command for that.

```sh
groundtrack service status
groundtrack service install --agent codex --agent claude
groundtrack service stop --agent claude
groundtrack service start --agent claude
groundtrack service restart
groundtrack service uninstall
```

Workers use explicit agent-home and repository-registry paths, independent of the
current shell directory. New project enrollment refreshes other enabled workers;
after manually removing/changing registry entries, restart the services to apply
the changed scope. Logs contain sanitized NDJSON summaries, not transcript bodies,
and rotate at 4 MiB with two backups. Scope registry, logs, locks and cached
binaries live under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/groundtrack` (default `~/.config/groundtrack`).
OS locks prevent duplicate managed workers and release on crashes. Stop disables
login startup until start/restart; uninstall removes only verified, owned job
definitions and retains logs, binaries and repository registrations. Process
supervision does not persist preview deduplication: each restart remains a fresh
preview run. Upgrading the watcher requires rerunning setup/service install.

For local development before a native release is published:

```sh
cargo build --release -p groundtrack-cli
node packages/hooks/dist/groundtrack.js service install --agent codex --agent claude --native-binary target/release/groundtrack-native
```

The native release workflow runs before the existing npm publication. Native
assets stay in the private source repository as a build cache; the authenticated
release job bundles all supported binaries in the existing public npm package.
Ordinary installs do not need GitHub access or credentials. This trades a larger
npm package for simple, offline-capable installation without additional packages
or publisher configuration. Native assets are immutable; when native source or the build recipe changes after release, bump both the
CLI package version and `NATIVE_VERSION` in `src/service/native.ts`. The workflow
rejects reuse of a version for a different native source tree.

The same package provides `groundtrack-hook`. Setup installs this shared runtime
once if needed for Claude, Codex, or Cursor. OpenCode uses
`@groundtrack/opencode-plugin` instead. Repeat runs use the installed runtime
without querying npm for updates on every invocation.

The CLI validates JSON/JSONC and TOML, preserves unrelated settings and comments,
reuses existing Groundtrack aliases, and backs up changed files before applying
atomic writes. Backups and selections live under
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/groundtrack` (default `~/.config/groundtrack`). Backups may
contain existing private configuration, so their directory and files are private.
A failure rolls back completed writes where possible and reports the backup
location. Malformed configuration, symbolic links, disabled connections/hooks,
and endpoint conflicts are reported for the affected agent. Other independent
selected agents can still be configured. Adding agents does not uninstall others.

## Connection and verification

When an upload service is configured (even if stopped), ordinary preview setup cannot enroll
a new repository into its shared registry. Use `setup --no-service` for hooks
only, or explicitly approve the scope with `service install --upload --yes`.

### Native automatic sync (explicit opt-in)

Cursor is supported alongside Codex and Claude. Its worker observes transcript
files and SQLite/WAL metadata changes, then uses the same durable outbox and
private upload policy. Set `CURSOR_HOME`, `CURSOR_STATE_DB`, or
`CURSOR_PROJECTS_DIR` before installation to override storage locations; managed
jobs capture the paths, not credentials. Missing headers/metadata fail closed.
OpenCode uses native database/WAL events and the installed CLI. It discovers the
storage path through `opencode db path`, refreshes metadata on relevant changes,
and exports only settled, scoped sessions into the shared outbox.
Set `OPENCODE_BIN` or `XDG_DATA_HOME` before installation for custom locations;
jobs preserve captured CLI/data paths. `service install --agent opencode
--reconcile-seconds 300` configures the slower recovery scan (five minutes by
default; `--poll-seconds` is a compatibility alias). No direct SQLite data reader
or new OpenCode server/plugin is needed.

Automatic uploads are separate from initial setup consent. Create an import-only
automatic-sync key in Settings, configure it with `groundtrack-native sync
configure --key-file PATH` (or piped `--key-stdin`), then run:

```sh
groundtrack service install --agent codex --agent claude --upload --yes
groundtrack service install --agent cursor --upload --yes
groundtrack service install --agent opencode --upload --yes
groundtrack service install --agent codex --preview
```

Keys are kept in private local credential files; the service definition gets only
the profile path. New setup remains preview-only. Existing explicit upload mode
is preserved during updates, and `--preview` deliberately disables uploading for
a selected service. The Rust outbox keeps latest complete snapshots and private
receipts across restarts, with retry/backoff, scoped identity checks and a bounded
local backlog. See the native CLI README for storage/retention limits and key
rotation. No production upload is performed merely by installing this package.

A local check verifies configuration, not a live authenticated host. Status
reports `configured` and `activation: unverified`; it never infers a connection
from a generated file. Each agent must load the connection and its hooks.

Interactive setup checks native sign-in requirements first. Claude Code must
approve a new project MCP server before OAuth; setup shows that action instead
of attempting a login that will fail. Codex can authenticate the selected endpoint
with a one-command configuration override while project and hook trust remain
explicit user actions. Existing Claude/OpenCode authentication is reused when
the client reports it, and successful logins are reflected in the final summary.
Use `--connect` to retry native sign-in for selected clients. Cursor and
desktop-only installations show their UI steps. In unattended runs, setup prints instructions and never blocks waiting
for OAuth. `--json` returns structured results without configuration contents or
credentials; use `--yes` to apply an explicitly selected setup.

Codex requires review and trust of the Groundtrack hook through `/hooks` or its
hook approval UI. New Codex setups use `.codex/hooks.json`; existing inline
hooks in `.codex/config.toml` are recognized and repaired without duplicating
them. Claude's `CLAUDE.md` imports the shared `AGENTS.md` policy. The plugin is
added to the existing OpenCode JSON/JSONC configuration.

Claude setup also installs a synchronous `SessionStart` check in project settings.
At startup, resume, clear, or fork it checks local MCP configuration and Claude's
own `mcp get` status. If Groundtrack is missing, disabled, awaiting approval,
unauthenticated, or not connected, Claude shows a warning with a repair command
and gives the agent the same context. An incomplete OAuth flow can leave Claude
in `Needs authentication` even when `mcp get` exits successfully; this state is
not treated as connected. The check never starts OAuth or blocks the session on
failure; its native probe has a five-second limit. It needs Claude project hooks
to be enabled and trusted, and is not a replacement for a live tool call. Other
clients still rely on their own setup and diagnostics.

In each selected agent, ask:

> Verify Groundtrack's connection and hook context with search_experiences.

The returned hook-context and instruction-version warnings determine whether
live activation needs attention. No synthetic engineering event is required.

## Doctor compatibility

`groundtrack doctor` is an alias for `status`; `groundtrack doctor --fix` uses the
same setup and repair flow. Doctor checks for a newer published hooks package;
when one is available, upgrade before repairing with an older bundled policy.
If the registry is unavailable, Doctor still checks local configuration and
preserves managed instructions newer than its own template. When invoked through
`npx`, Doctor checks the globally installed hook runtime rather than the
temporary executable provided by `npx`. Existing single-client commands continue to work:

```sh
groundtrack doctor --fix --client codex
```

The lower-level `runDoctor` API remains for existing consumers. New setup uses
client-specific plans for MCP, hooks/plugins, and instructions, so it can preview
and repair several selected agents safely.

## Local impact skill (opt-in)

The package includes a read-only `groundtrack-impact` skill for Claude Code and
Codex. It audits local sessions to produce an evidence-backed report on how
Groundtrack changed your work. **Setup does not install or invoke this skill**;
install it explicitly only when you want to give an agent access to local
transcripts. From this repository checkout, choose either or both agents:

```sh
mkdir -p "${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills"
cp -R packages/hooks/skills/groundtrack-impact "${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills/"
mkdir -p "${CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR:-$HOME/.claude}/skills"
cp -R packages/hooks/skills/groundtrack-impact "${CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR:-$HOME/.claude}/skills/"
```

If `@groundtrack/hooks` is installed in another project, use
`node_modules/@groundtrack/hooks/skills/groundtrack-impact` as the copy source
instead. For Claude Code, set this copied skill to **user-only** in `/skills`
(or set `"groundtrack-impact": "user-invocable-only"` under `skillOverrides` in
Claude settings) before using it; that prevents Claude from loading this
transcript-reading workflow on its own. Codex's packaged `agents/openai.yaml` already
disables implicit invocation. Restart your agent if needed, then explicitly invoke
`$groundtrack-impact` in Codex or `/groundtrack-impact` in Claude Code and
authorize the session scope. The audit reads Claude
sessions from `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (default `~/.claude`) and Codex sessions from
`CODEX_HOME` (default `~/.codex`); it never uploads transcripts or runs the
session-import command. The agent's model provider may receive selected local
context during analysis.

## Import coding-agent sessions

Import completed Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode sessions with an API key created in Groundtrack
Settings. The default scope is the current Git repository; subagents and files modified
in the last five minutes are excluded. Groundtrack reads Codex sessions from `CODEX_HOME`
(default `~/.codex`), Claude sessions from `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (default `~/.claude`),
and Cursor transcripts from `CURSOR_HOME` (default `~/.cursor`). Cursor metadata comes from
its local `state.vscdb`; set `CURSOR_STATE_DB` to override that database path. Cursor import
is CLI-only and requires unflagged `node:sqlite` support (Node.js 22.13+, 23.4+, or 24+).
OpenCode import invokes the installed `opencode` CLI (override it with `OPENCODE_BIN`) and uses
private temporary files for its session inventory and exports. This avoids OpenCode's large piped
export truncation while ensuring the unsanitized source export is removed after local pruning.

```sh
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --dry-run
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --yes
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --agent claude --dry-run
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --agent claude --all-repos --yes
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --agent cursor --dry-run
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --agent cursor --all-repos --yes
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --agent opencode --dry-run
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack import --agent opencode --all-repos --yes
```

The command streams source files through a deterministic privacy filter before upload.
Reasoning, system/developer instructions, turn context other than the model name, and
recognized credentials are removed locally. Uploads are sequential and retry only
transient failures. Successful imports are recorded atomically under
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/groundtrack`; receipts are scoped to the endpoint, API-key fingerprint,
visibility, source hash, and canonicalization version. Use `--json` for one machine-readable
result object and `--url` for a preview or self-hosted deployment.

Imported transcripts are private by default. Groundtrack analyzes completed imports and may add
high-confidence extracted lessons—not transcript content—to the organization's shared knowledge.
Changing transcript visibility does not change this learning behavior; deleting an imported
session retracts its derived knowledge.

## Watch completed sessions

`groundtrack watch --once` is the sync engine behind a future scheduled watcher.
One pass scans session file metadata, compares it with a durable cursor, and only
reads and uploads files whose size or modification time changed. Files modified in
the last five minutes stay `active`; once they are quiet, the pass prunes and
uploads them using the same privacy filter and receipts as `import`.

```sh
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack watch --once --agent codex --dry-run
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack watch --once --agent codex --all-repos --yes
GROUNDTRACK_API_KEY=... groundtrack watch --once --agent claude --all-repos --yes
```

The cursor lives at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/groundtrack/watch-state-<source>.json` (mode
`0600`). Unchanged files are not reopened, rehashed, or re-uploaded. A preview
without `--yes` does not write cursor state. Only one watch pass can run per source
at a time; a stale PID lock is recovered automatically. The loop, filesystem
events, and an OS timer are intentionally not part of `--once`.

Codex paginated sessions are merged before upload. The watcher groups rollout
pages by `session_id`, follows the `history_base.thread_id` chain, and uploads one
complete snapshot. A chain with a missing or still-live page is reported instead
of uploading a fragment.

`templates/AGENTS.md` is the source of truth for the managed repository policy.
After changing it, run `pnpm sync:agent-instructions`; tests reject drift between
the setup guide, this repository's managed `AGENTS.md` block, and the packaged template.

## Development

Agent IDs, names, aliases, event sources, enrichment kinds, and session-import
capabilities are defined once in `src/agents.ts`, exported as
`@groundtrack/hooks/agents`. The CLI, web UI, hooks, and server consume that
catalog and its derived types. Keep it dependency-free so browser bundles can
load it without the Node-only hook runtime.

Build and test the CLI from the repository:

```sh
pnpm --filter @groundtrack/hooks build
node packages/hooks/dist/groundtrack.js setup --repo /path/to/test-project
pnpm --filter @groundtrack/hooks test
```

With Claude Code and Codex installed, also run the isolated native-client
preflight checks (they do not start OAuth or touch your normal agent profiles):

```sh
GROUNDTRACK_TEST_NATIVE_CLIENTS=1 pnpm --filter @groundtrack/hooks test
```

The `groundtrack-hook` command reads a pre-tool-use hook payload from standard input and enriches
Groundtrack `store_event` and `search_experiences` calls with:

- the client session and model identifiers (using Claude's host-provided
  transcript path when its hook payload omits the model);
- for `store_event`, a stable client event id derived from the host's tool invocation id; and
- repository, branch, commit, and dirty-worktree context collected with Git.

The Git context is collected from the hook's working directory (or a single
Cursor workspace root) and overrides model-provided values. Collection fails
open when the hook is outside a Git worktree. The command does not send network
requests.

Update it with:

```bash
npm update -g @groundtrack/hooks
```
